newsitem.title: USA: U.S. cites progress in Guatemala's labor laws.
newsitem.headline: U.S. cites progress in Guatemala's labor laws.

text.p: The United States said on Friday it was ending its review of Guatemala's eligibility for trade preferences, saying the Central American country had made significant progress in curbing violations of workers' rights.

But Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said further advances were needed and warned Guatemala City that the United States would continue to monitor the treatment of workers and would begin a new review if there was serious retrogression.
The review was begun in 1992 after allegations -- some from U.S. labor unions -- that Guatemala failed to provide internationally recognized workers rights.
Barshefsky said in a statement that the most noteworthy progress during the review had been made since President Alvaro Arzu took office 15 months ago.
Arzu's presidency, she said, had been "characterized by a dramatic reduction of the intimidation of workers and their leaders."
The lifting of the review, a major irritant to Guatemalan governments, came just two days before Secretary of State Madeleine Albright was to visit Guatemala.

In her statement, Barshefsky said the Guatemalan government had developed administrative remedies to deal with labor law violations, procedures for the registration of unions had been simplified and the Labor Ministry had doubled the number of labor inspectors and improved training.
"The Ministry of Labor has endeavored to change the traditional confrontational and politicized relationship between labor, business and government," she said.

Barshefsky cited as cause for continuing concern the inefficiency of the judiciary in dealing promptly with labor cases, but noted that the number of courts dealing with labor issues was being increased and decentralized.
The GSP is a program that grants duty-free treatment to specified products that are imported from more than 140 designated developing countries.
